title: Tall, Long Fingers, Early Diastolic Murmur / Look Beyond the Heart

blocks.text: Tall, Long Fingers, Early Diastolic Murmur / Look Beyond the Heart

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-12 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease (Circulation 2022); 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases (Eur Heart J 2024) · Related AMaC: AMaC aortic regurgitation station; this one tests a connective tissue cause
The patient is a man of 24 who studies engineering. He was sent by his optician because of a family history of heart problems. Please examine his cardiovascular system to establish the cause.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A tall young man with long fingers and an early diastolic murmur is most likely Marfan syndrome. The station turns on seeing the body as well as the heart.
The Examiner Trap. Candidates go straight to the chest and call it aortic regurgitation. Pass: body signs first, then the murmur, then the aortic root and the dissection warning. Fail: murmur only.

rows: Look at the whole person first: height, limbs, fingers, chest wall, palate, spine and feet.
"May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; build, arm span, hands, thumb and wrist signs, palate, pulse.
Pulse and pulse pressure first, then listen with him leaning forward in held expiration.
"I'm going to listen over the heart, then lean you forward and ask you to breathe out."
Collapsing pulse; apex; thrill; four areas; leaning forward; lung bases; sacrum; spine; ankles; cover him.
Name the syndrome, the valve lesion and the danger, and say where he needs follow-up.
"He has features of Marfan syndrome with aortic regurgitation. The aortic root needs measuring."
Present in order; diagnosis; echo; root size; family testing; thank him.
Starts without consent; presses hard on the chest; leaves him exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone, keeps exposure to the minimum, and checks he is comfortable leaning forward.
Disorganised; goes to the chest and omits the build, hands, pulse or leaning-forward position.
Looks at build, arm span, hands, thumb and wrist signs and palate, then pulse, apex, four auscultation areas leaning forward, bases, spine and ankles.
Also checks feet, skin stretch marks and the eyes for lens dislocation.
Reports signs that are not present, or finds only the murmur.
Finds tall build, long fingers, positive thumb and wrist signs, pectus excavatum, high palate, scoliosis, collapsing pulse and an early diastolic murmur.
Also finds a displaced apex, flat feet and a wide pulse pressure, and states no stigmata of endocarditis.
Calls it aortic regurgitation only, or rheumatic heart disease.
Also separates Marfan from homocystinuria and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and gives the Ghent criteria as the basis for diagnosis.
Names aortic root dilatation, dissection, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, lens dislocation and pneumothorax.
Also names retinal detachment and dural ectasia.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): calls sudden tearing chest or back pain muscular and sends him home with painkillers.
Says echocardiography measures the root, treats with a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker, tests relatives, and sends tearing pain to emergency care.
Also gives individualised exercise advice, encouraging moderate aerobic exercise, and explains that surgery is timed by root size, growth rate and family history, as a specialist decision.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: tall and thin; respiratory rate 14; pulse 78 regular and collapsing; blood pressure 142/58; SpO2 99% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Arm span greater than height. Hands: long fingers; thumb and wrist signs positive; no splinter haemorrhages. Palate: high-arched. Pectus excavatum; mild scoliosis; flat feet. JVP not raised. Apex beat displaced to the sixth space, anterior axillary line; no thrill. Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder leaning forward in held expiration. Lungs clear. No oedema.
Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Complications? (E) 4. Investigation? (E) 5. Management? (E)

Curveballs: He asks if his children will have it: autosomal dominant, half the children, genetic testing. Sudden tearing chest or back pain: emergency, possible aortic dissection. Can he play football? Exercise advice is individualised (ESC 2024): moderate aerobic exercise is encouraged.
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and asks about pain (G)
Looks at build, arm span, hands and palate before the chest (A)
Feels the pulse for a collapsing character (A)
Finds thumb and wrist signs, pectus and scoliosis (B)
Finds an early diastolic murmur leaning forward in held expiration (B)
Names Marfan syndrome with aortic regurgitation (D)
Lists root dilatation, dissection, mitral prolapse, lens dislocation and pneumothorax (E)
Requests echocardiography and says the root is measured (E)
Names a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker and relative testing (E)
Says tearing chest or back pain needs emergency care (E)
Covers him, cleans hands and thanks him (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Sit back. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens lying flat only.) [R2 Fail] A systolic murmur. [R3 Fail] Rheumatic aortic valve disease. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Complications and warning signs?
CANDIDATE: Heart failure. [R5 Fail] Sudden back pain is muscular; give painkillers. [R6 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): the examiner sees a red flag, because tearing chest or back pain is a possible dissection and needs emergency care. No consent, no body signs, and the syndrome missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Build, arm span, hands, thumb and wrist signs, palate; pulse, apex, four areas leaning forward, bases, spine, ankles.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: He is tall with long fingers, positive thumb and wrist signs, pectus excavatum, a high palate, scoliosis, a collapsing pulse and an early diastolic murmur. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Marfan syndrome with aortic regurgitation. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Complications?
CANDIDATE: Root dilatation, dissection, mitral prolapse, lens dislocation and pneumothorax. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Management?
CANDIDATE: Echocardiography to measure the root; a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker; test relatives. Tearing chest or back pain goes to emergency care. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not separate Marfan from other causes, name the Ghent criteria or explain how surgery is timed.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) May I examine your heart? Would you like a chaperone? I'll keep you covered and check you are comfortable leaning forward. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Build, arm span, hands, thumb and wrist signs, palate, feet, stretch marks, eyes; pulse; four areas leaning forward in held expiration; spine; ankles.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Tall, long fingers, thumb and wrist signs, pectus, scoliosis, flat feet, wide pulse pressure, displaced apex, early diastolic murmur; no endocarditis stigmata. [R3 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Marfan syndrome with aortic regurgitation, not homocystinuria or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome; the Ghent criteria and genetic testing confirm it. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Complications?
CANDIDATE: Root dilatation, dissection, regurgitation, mitral prolapse, lens dislocation, retinal detachment, dural ectasia and pneumothorax. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Management?

CANDIDATE: Regular echo for root size, at least annually and more often if the root is 45 mm or more or growing; beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker; surgery is timed by root size, growth rate and family history, so a specialist decision; exercise advice individualised, with moderate aerobic exercise encouraged (ESC 2024); test relatives. Tearing pain is an emergency. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands, thanks him.) [R1 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, feet, skin and eyes, the differential, the Ghent criteria, how surgery is timed, activity advice and relative testing.
R2: Going straight to the chest. The diagnosis is made from the body, and the signs in the hands, palate and spine are missed.
R4: Naming aortic regurgitation alone. The syndrome decides the root surveillance and the relative testing.
R5: Naming heart failure only. Root dilatation and dissection are the danger in Marfan syndrome.
R6: Not saying tearing pain needs emergency care. A missed dissection can kill him today.
"Let me look at his hands and palate again before I go on."
"He is tall with long fingers, so I'd say Marfan syndrome with aortic regurgitation."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"
Marfan syndrome: autosomal dominant fibrillin-1 disorder. Diagnosis uses the revised Ghent criteria (2010): aortic root enlargement, lens dislocation, systemic features and genetic testing.

Timing of aortic root surgery depends on diameter, growth rate, family history of dissection and valve disease, and is decided by a specialist aortic team; in Marfan syndrome surgery is indicated at a sinus diameter of 50 mm or more (ESC 2024; 5.0 cm in ACC/AHA 2022) and should be considered from 45 mm with additional risk factors: family history of dissection at a small diameter, resistant hypertension, or growth of 3 mm a year or more (ESC 2024). A beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker is used to slow growth.

Echo surveillance: at least annually if the root is under 45 mm with no risk factors, at least every 6 months if under 45 mm with risk factors, and every 6 to 12 months at 45 mm or more (ESC 2024). Test first-degree relatives; individualise activity advice by aortic diameter, family history and fitness, with regular moderate aerobic exercise encouraged (ESC 2024); pre-conception counselling.
THINK: Tall, long fingers, diastolic murmur: Marfan.
SAY: "Marfan syndrome with aortic regurgitation."
DO: Body first; lean forward in held expiration.
NUMBERS: Surgery timed by root size, growth and family history: 50 mm or more in Marfan, consider from 45 mm with risk factors (ESC 2024; ACC/AHA 2022 5.0 cm).
TRAP: Murmur only; missing the dissection.
FINISH: Echo, beta-blocker, relatives; tearing pain is an emergency.

2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease. Circulation 2022. https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106 Supports: surgical timing (5.0 cm; 4.5 cm with high-risk features) in Marfan syndrome.

2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases. Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538-3700. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehae179 Supports: Marfan syndrome recommendation tables 60 to 64: echo surveillance intervals, beta-blocker or ARB, root surgery at 50 mm or more (45 mm with risk factors), individualised exercise.

Marfan syndrome. GeNotes (NHS England Genomic Education Programme). https://www.genomicseducation.hee.nhs.uk/genotes/ Supports: Surveillance, cascade testing, sport advice and pre-conception counselling.
